_comment: The ideal closed-loop homestead OUTLINE (one person). Operator directives: 2026-07-05 'use Home as a page for outlining what we need in the perfect ideal 100% closed loop self-sustaining homestead'; same day: dual units 'metric (imperial)' so either background reads it instantly, plus TWO TIERS per loop: bare minimum vs a life of luxury with all the latest tech (assume comfort in space, not austerity). Every requirement carries tier: 'baseline' or 'luxury'. game_id is a REAL id in the game data (unit-test enforced) OR the empty string, which renders as a 'not in game yet' flag: the luxury tier doubles as the game-content gap list, exactly the operator's stated purpose. Rendered by BOTH the native Home page (src/gui/pages/homes.rs) and the web mirror (web/pages/home.html fetches /data/home_outline.json). Infinite-of-X: edit here, both surfaces update. Top-level data/ so the web deploy publishes it. No em dashes in copy (operator rule). AUDITED 2026-07-30 (life-support balance pass): every loop was re-derived from first principles per person per day against NASA life-support baselines, BIOS-3, NREL NSRDB, FAO/WHO/UNU, FAO-56, and the repo's own data/plants.csv, data/food/crop_nutrition.ron, data/self_sufficiency/location.ron, data/machines/home_solo.ron and docs/design/homestead.md. Numbers that did not balance were corrected here and the correction is stated in the loop's balance array. The nutrients loop was found NOT to close and is now flagged closes:false, which is the honest finding, not a regression. New per-loop fields 'balance' and 'assumptions' and the top-level 'assumptions' carry the arithmetic; NEITHER RENDERER READS THEM YET (see in_game_next).
title: The ideal closed-loop homestead
subtitle: One person, seven loops, two tiers: the bare minimum that keeps you alive, and a life of luxury with all the latest tech. Both honestly sized, in metric and imperial, for a named place.
intro: 100% closure is physically impossible (entropy always leaks), but a single person CAN close energy, water, air, climate, and nearly all food. Every number below is a balance: what goes out per person per day against what comes back, with the assumption set beside it, because an unstated assumption makes a balance unfalsifiable. Where a loop does not close, it says so and states the size of the residual. Nutrients is the one that genuinely does not close, and phosphorus is why. What one home cannot close is listed last, on purpose: those gaps are why community and trade exist.
assumptions: PLACE: Silverdale, WA, USA, about 47.6 N, the site already named in data/self_sufficiency/location.ron. Everything below is sized for open Earth at that site unless a loop calls out the sealed mothership case separately. Move the homestead and most of these numbers move with it.

SUN: NREL NSRDB / PVWatts for Puget Sound gives 3.9 peak sun hours per day annual average (regional range 3.5 to 4.2), about 6.0 in June and about 1.3 to 1.5 in December. An off-grid array is sized for December, never for the annual average.

PV DERATE: 0.75 end to end, being 0.86 (PVWatts default system losses) x 0.96 (inverter) x 0.91 (battery round trip), because in an off-grid home most energy is time shifted through the battery. The older 0.80 figure omitted the battery round trip.
OCCUPANT: one adult, moderately active (FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 Human Energy Requirements, physical activity level 1.75), which is what homestead labour actually is.

CLIMATE: 2,610 heating degree days base 18.3 C (68 F) and 44 cooling degree days, both in Celsius days. Note that location.ron records 4,700 HDD against a stated 18.3 C base; 4,700 is the Fahrenheit day figure base 65 F, so the file mixes conventions. 4,700 F days divided by 1.8 is the 2,610 C days used here.

SHELL: the ten room house of docs/design/homestead.md section 3, 16 x 20 m (52 x 66 ft) on one storey with 3 m (10 ft) ceilings, high performance envelope: walls U 0.15, roof U 0.10, floor U 0.15, triple glazing U 0.80 W/m2K, heat recovery ventilation at 85%.

CROPPING: sun lit greenhouse, no supplemental lighting, so November to February is a light famine that storage covers rather than production. Outdoor field is dry farmed, which is standard practice here because the growing season IS the dry season.
The five open loops in data/self_sufficiency/cannot_close.ron stay open. Nothing in this audit closed any of them, and the nutrients finding below makes the raw chemistry entry stronger, not weaker.

loops.name: Power
loops.demand: Bare minimum 4.0 kWh/day, duty cycle honest: air recycler 0.60, aquaponic air pump 1.20, cooking 0.60, cold storage and chargers 0.70, tower pumps 0.27, lighting 0.20, water pump plus purifier plus irrigation 0.17, hot water off the biomass stove and no washing machine. A life of luxury runs 16.0 kWh/day: the 4.0 baseline plus climate 5.0, hot water on demand 2.0, fridge and freezer 1.5, washer and dryer 1.0, computers and entertainment 1.5, kitchen appliances 0.3, 3D printer 0.2, power tools 0.5. Peak draw is a separate problem from energy and was never stated before: about 3.9 kW at bare minimum (a 2.4 kW oven plus a kettle) and about 7 kW at luxury.
loops.closure_note: Sized for DECEMBER, because that is the month that decides an off-grid array. One 400 W panel at this site yields 1.17 kWh/day annual average and 0.39 kWh/day in December (0.4 kW x 1.3 sun hours x 0.75 derate). Bare minimum needs 4.0 divided by 0.39, which is 10.3, so 11 panels: 4.29 kWh/day in December plus 0.7 kWh/day of wind, a 25 percent margin in the worst month and a 3.4x surplus in summer that you simply dump. CORRECTED FROM 4 PANELS: the old figure assumed 4.5 sun hours and named no location; at the site this design actually names, 4 panels deliver 1.56 kWh/day in December against a 4.0 kWh/day load, a 43 percent shortfall held for about 90 days, roughly 157 kWh per winter that no 8 kWh battery can carry. Storage is now sized to a 5 day overcast stretch at 0.4 sun hours, which is a 9.9 kWh hole, so 3 banks and 12 kWh rather than 2 and 8. Luxury keeps deep winter on the biomass stove, so its December electrical load is 11.0 kWh/day, needing 28 panels and 10 banks; heating December with the heat pump instead would need 39 panels. The residual is generator fuel: a biodigester on 1.5 kg/day of feedstock makes about 0.25 m3 of biogas per day, roughly 0.37 kWh/day of electricity through a 25 percent efficient genset, which is about one 2 hour generator run per week and NOT the whole winter tail. The claim that the biodigester brews the generator's fuel was over stated by roughly 3x; the rest of that fuel is traded.
balance: Supply per panel: 0.400 kW x 3.9 sun-h x 0.75 = 1.17 kWh/day annual; 0.400 kW x 1.3 sun-h x 0.75 = 0.39 kWh/day December.
Baseline: 11 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 wind = 4.99 kWh/day December vs 4.00 kWh/day demand. Margin +0.99 kWh/day (+25%).
Baseline annual: 11 x 1.17 + 0.7 = 13.6 kWh/day vs 4.0. Surplus 9.6 kWh/day, unavoidable when the array is winter sized.
Old spec check: 4 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 = 2.26 kWh/day December vs 4.00. DEFICIT 1.74 kWh/day for about 90 days = 157 kWh/winter.
Storage: 5 day overcast at 0.4 sun-h gives 11 x 0.12 + 0.7 = 2.02 kWh/day, deficit 1.98 x 5 = 9.9 kWh. 3 banks = 12 kWh usable. Closes.
Luxury December (biomass carrying heat): 11.0 kWh/day demand / 0.39 = 28.2, so 28 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 = 11.6 kWh/day. Margin +5%.
Luxury all electric December: 23.8 kWh/day demand would need 39 panels. Stated so the fork is visible.

Biogas: 1.5 kg/day feedstock x ~0.17 m3/kg = 0.25 m3 biogas at 60% CH4 = 0.15 m3 CH4 x 35.8 MJ/m3 = 5.4 MJ = 1.5 kWh thermal x 0.25 genset efficiency = 0.37 kWh/day electric, about 135 kWh/year, about 7% of the annual load.
Peak vs average: battery banks discharge 2 kW each, so 3 banks = 6 kW and a 2.4 kW oven is 40% of the bus. The old 2 bank spec gave 4 kW and the oven alone was 60% of it.
assumptions: NREL NSRDB Puget Sound: 3.9 peak sun hours annual, 6.0 June, 1.3 December.
Derate 0.75 = 0.86 PVWatts losses x 0.96 inverter x 0.91 battery round trip.
battery_bank capacity 4 kWh usable per bank, 2 kW charge and discharge (data/machines/home_solo.ron).
Biogas yield 0.15 to 0.25 m3 per kg of wet mixed food waste and humanure, methane fraction 0.55 to 0.65, small genset electrical efficiency 0.20 to 0.28.

requirements.why: 400 W each; 0.39 kWh/day in December and 1.17 kWh/day annual, sized for the worst month not the average
12 kWh usable, which is the 5 day overcast stretch plus a margin; 2 banks left a 2 kWh hole
0.7 kWh/day; 14% of the December supply, and it blows hardest exactly when the sun is worst
2 kW; biogas covers about one 2 hour run per week, the rest of the fuel is traded
11.6 kWh/day in December against the 11.0 kWh/day comfort load, with deep winter heat left on the stove
40 kWh, which is the 5 day overcast hole at comfort draw; 8 banks fell about 6 kWh short
peak is not energy: sheds the oven, heater, and workshop against the 20 kW bus so the array is sized for kWh, not for the worst simultaneous minute

loops.name: Water
loops.demand: Bare minimum 85 L/day (22 gal/day) net household, which is the actual fixture list and not a round number: drinking and cooking 5, kitchen sink 15, bathroom sink 5, shower 35, toilet 14, laundry 11. Luxury about 120 L/day (32 gal/day) with long hot showers, more laundry, and a dishwasher. Irrigation is a real and much larger flow, about 455 L/day (120 gal/day) of evapotranspiration off the greenhouse canopy in the growing season, and it is NOT covered by greywater alone.
loops.closure_note: CORRECTED, and the correction matters: the old note claimed 155 L/day (41 gal/day) of greywater recovery against an 80 L/day household, which is 194 percent recovery and is physically impossible. That 155 figure is the three person home.ron number imported without scaling. One person's greywater producing fixtures are the kitchen sink, bathroom sink, shower, and laundry, totalling 66 L/day (17 gal/day); the toilet is blackwater and drinking water is consumed. At 90 percent recovery after filtration and settling that is 59 L/day (16 gal/day). Rain catchment was also a game port number rather than a physical one: 1,400 mm of annual rain on the 320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) house roof at a 0.85 runoff coefficient is 1,044 L/day (276 gal/day) on an annual average, but about 75 percent of it falls October to April, so the July and August dry stretch delivers only about 23 L/day (6 gal/day). The cistern is the machine that makes this work: a 90 day dry stretch draws 7,650 L against 2,040 L caught, a net 5,610 L (1,480 gal) drawdown on an 8,000 L (2,100 gal) tank, so it closes with 30 percent to spare and the well is the backstop. The term the old note omitted entirely is evapotranspiration: 350 m2 of greenhouse canopy at a season average 1.3 mm/day under glass transpires 455 L/day, which greywater covers only 13 percent of. It closes because a closed greenhouse condenses most of it back, the same 85 to 95 percent water closure BIOS-3 measured, leaving about 68 L/day (18 gal/day) of net irrigation demand that greywater then does cover. The outdoor field cannot be irrigated at this scale and is dry farmed, which is normal practice here.
balance: Household in: 85 L/day baseline, 120 L/day luxury.
Greywater out: kitchen 15 + bath sink 5 + shower 35 + laundry 11 = 66 L/day; x 0.90 recovery = 59 L/day. Recovery ratio 59/85 = 69%, which is physically possible. The old 155/80 = 194% was not.
Rain catchment: 1.400 m x 320 m2 x 0.85 = 381 m3/year = 1,044 L/day annual average; dry stretch (about 75 mm over 90 days) = 2,040 L total = 23 L/day.
Dry season drawdown: 85 x 90 = 7,650 L used, 2,040 L caught, net 5,610 L against an 8,000 L cistern. Margin 2,390 L (30%).
Autonomy: 8,000 / 85 = 94 days baseline; 8,000 / 120 = 67 days luxury.
Greenhouse evapotranspiration: FAO-56 reference ET0 about 2.0 mm/day season average outdoors, x 0.65 under glass = 1.3 mm/day; 350 m2 x 1.3 = 455 L/day, peaking about 805 L/day in July.
Condensate recovery at 85% leaves 455 x 0.15 = 68 L/day net, which the 59 L/day of greywater plus catchment covers.
Well backstop: 2.0 L/min = 2,880 L/day when run, so it refills a day's household use in 30 minutes.
assumptions: Fixture flows are the per person figures already in data/machines/home_solo.ron as of v0.1027.
Runoff coefficient 0.85 for a metal or membrane roof; 1,400 mm annual rainfall from data/self_sufficiency/location.ron.
FAO-56 Penman Monteith reference ET0 for Puget Sound, greenhouse crop coefficient bundled into the 0.65 under glass factor.
Condensate recovery 85%, the mid of the 80 to 95% range closed greenhouses and BIOS-3 achieved.

requirements.why: 8,000 L (2,100 gal); 94 days of autonomy and the 5,610 L (1,480 gal) dry season drawdown is what sizes it
320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) of roof at 0.85 runoff; 1,044 L/day annual average but only 23 L/day in the August dry stretch
2 L/min (0.5 gal/min); refills a day's household use in 30 minutes and is the dry season backstop
240 L/day (63 gal/day) potable polish, 2.8x the one person need
the six fixtures that sum to the real 85 L/day: cistern to pump to purifier to taps
recovers 59 L/day (16 gal/day) from sinks, shower, and laundry, which is 69% of intake; the old 155 L/day claim exceeded intake and could not exist
the loop that makes irrigation affordable: recovers about 85% of the 455 L/day (120 gal/day) the canopy transpires, the same closure BIOS-3 measured
heat pump water heater, about 2 kWh/day for one person; at bare minimum this duty sits on the biomass stove instead
with a heat pump dryer, about 1 kWh/day and 11 L/day averaged
modern units use LESS water than hand washing, about 10 L (2.6 gal) per load, so it is close to water neutral against the kitchen sink

loops.name: Food
loops.demand: 2,600 kcal/day and about 75 g (2.6 oz) of protein, one moderately active adult, both tiers. CORRECTED FROM 2,200 kcal and 55 g: FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 puts a 70 kg adult male at physical activity level 1.75 at 2,900 kcal/day and a 57 kg adult female at 2,250, and homestead labour is not sedentary. Harvest must exceed intake by about 15 percent to cover the seed fraction and storage losses, so the real target is about 3,000 kcal/day of harvest. Luxury adds variety, spice, and serious preservation, not more calories.
loops.closure_note: The honest cap is light, and the light has to be measured, not asserted. Annual photosynthetically active radiation under glass at this site is about 20.2 mol/m2/day, but December is 6.7 mol/m2/day, below the 12 to 17 mol/m2/day leafy greens need and far below the 20 to 30 fruiting crops need: November to February the sun lit greenhouse holds, it does not produce, and four months of eating come out of the silo and the root cellar. Realised food energy for a well run unlit greenhouse here is about 7.2 kcal/m2/day, roughly two to three times the 2.4 to 3.4 kcal/m2/day that the biointensive benchmark of 700 to 1,000 m2 per person actually represents. THE BIG CORRECTION: the old note argued that because the garden room is 1,156 m2 (12,440 sq ft) it clears the 700 to 1,000 m2 bar, but a room is not a canopy. Counting the machines actually placed in data/machines/home_solo.ron gives 16 m2 of potato bed, 6 m2 of oilseed bed, 4 m2 of grain tray, about 18 m2 of tower canopy, and 2.6 m2 of tank, which is about 44 m2 (474 sq ft) of lit canopy, 3.8 percent of the floor. At 7.2 kcal/m2/day that is 317 kcal/day, not the claimed 2,078 kcal/day; even crediting the full 116 m2 of lit floor the array spacing reserves, it is 835 kcal/day. The indoor claim was over by 2.5x to 6.5x. What actually closes the loop is area that was never written down: about 350 m2 (3,770 sq ft) of greenhouse canopy plus 1,600 to 2,000 m2 (0.16 to 0.20 ha, 0.40 to 0.49 acre) of arable including rotation. That arable figure lands on FAO's global arable per capita of 0.19 ha, which is a good independent check. Protein was never the binding constraint and closes with margin at about 103 g/day from the grain and legume pairing. The open edge nobody costed is fish feed: 55 kg/year of tilapia at a feed conversion ratio of 1.5 to 2.0 needs 85 to 110 kg/year of feed, which must come from duckweed or azolla on their own 20 to 40 m2 of lit water, plus worms and crop waste, or be bought.
balance: Light cap: 3.9 kWh/m2/day x 3.6 MJ/kWh x 0.45 PAR fraction x 4.57 umol/J = 28.9 mol/m2/day outdoors; x 0.70 glazing = 20.2 mol/m2/day annual under glass. December: 1.3 kWh/m2/day gives 6.7 mol/m2/day under glass.
Realised yield: biointensive 700 to 1,000 m2 per person at 2,400 kcal/day = 2.4 to 3.4 kcal/m2/day. Unlit greenhouse here about 7.2 kcal/m2/day (range 5 to 10).
Canopy as instantiated: 8 potato beds x 2 m2 = 16, 3 oilseed x 2 = 6, 2 grain trays x 2 = 4, 9 towers x ~2 m2 leaf projected = 18, tank 2.6. Total about 44 m2 in a 1,156 m2 room.
Indoor supply, honest: 44 m2 x 7.2 = 317 kcal/day. Claimed 2,078 kcal/day. Over by 6.5x on canopy, 2.5x if the full 116 m2 of lit floor is credited.

Potato bed cross-check: +120 kcal/day from 2.0 m2 = 60 kcal/m2/day = 21,900 kcal/m2/year; at 770 kcal/kg (crop_nutrition.ron potato 77 kcal/100 g) that is 28.4 kg/m2/year = 284 t/ha/year, against 50 t/ha per season for the best commercial field crop and 70 to 100 t/ha per cycle for aeroponic seed potato under continuous lamps. Sun lit here the honest figure is 45 to 60 kcal/day per bed.

Potato plant-count cross-check: plants.csv potato is 90 growth_days at 4 to 10 yield units, crop_nutrition.ron is 150 g/unit, so one plant gives 600 to 1,500 g per cycle, mid 1,050 g = 11.7 g/day = 9 kcal/day. 120 kcal/day therefore needs 13.3 plants in 2 m2 = 6.7 plants/m2 against a real intensive 4 to 6 plants/m2.

Variety tower cross-check: +92 kcal/day on the 2.2 x 2.2 m array spacing = 4.84 m2 of lit floor each = 19 kcal/m2/day = 6,930 kcal/m2/year, about 8x the best biointensive figure. Honest sun lit figure is 25 to 40 kcal/day per tower.

Grain field area, derived because it was never stated: western Washington winter wheat at 4 to 6 t/ha = 0.5 kg/m2/year x 3,400 kcal/kg = 1,700 kcal/m2/year = 4.7 kcal/m2/day, so +3,100 kcal/day needs 660 m2 in crop.

Legume field area: dry bean at 2 t/ha = 0.2 kg/m2/year x 3,330 kcal/kg = 666 kcal/m2/year = 1.8 kcal/m2/day, so +700 kcal/day needs 384 m2 in crop. Both fields are 2.4 x 2.4 m boxes in the data, which is a marker, not an area.

Protein: legume 700 kcal/day = 210 g dry bean x 21.6 g/100 g = 45 g; grain eaten 1,200 kcal/day = 353 g wheat x 13.7 g/100 g = 48 g; garden about 10 g. Total 103 g/day against a 75 g/day target. Closes.

B12 and omega 3: 2.4 ug/day of B12 needs about 150 g/day of tilapia at 1.6 ug/100 g = 55 kg/year, which a 2.56 m3 tank at 20 to 40 kg/m3/year supplies. Feed at FCR 1.5 to 2.0 is 85 to 110 kg/year and is NOT accounted for anywhere.
Seed fraction: modern wheat at a 150 kg/ha seeding rate on a 5 t/ha crop is 3%; saving open pollinated seed with a margin is 5 to 8%. Vegetables cost 5 to 10% of bed days rather than mass.
Storage losses (FAO post harvest, well managed): grain in a sealed silo 2 to 5%, roots and tubers in a root cellar 10 to 25% over a winter. Combined with seed, harvest must beat intake by about 15%.
assumptions: FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 Human Energy Requirements at physical activity level 1.75 for the calorie target; 1.0 to 1.2 g protein per kg body mass plus a 10% digestibility uplift for a largely plant based diet.
Light use efficiency 1.0 g dry biomass per mol PAR (published range 0.7 to 1.3 for well managed controlled environment crops).
Yields cross-checked against data/plants.csv growth_days and yield_min/yield_max and data/food/crop_nutrition.ron calories_per_100g and grams_per_yield_unit.
Garden wide harvest index about 0.45, so 45% of plant dry matter is edible.
No supplemental lighting. Lighting the canopy instead would cost 10 to 50 kWh/day, which data/machines/home_solo.ron already says and which the power loop cannot fund.

requirements.why: the number the old outline never wrote down; a 1,156 m2 room holding 44 m2 of canopy is not a 1,156 m2 garden
45 to 60 kcal/day each sun lit, not the catalogued 120, which needs 284 t/ha/year and year round lamps
25 to 40 kcal/day each sun lit, plus all the vegetables, vitamins, and plant protein across 32 real crops
fats from sunflower and flax; 584 kcal/100 g makes seed the densest thing the garden grows
100 kcal/day from dark vertical space; the only food that costs no light budget at all
55 kg/year of fish closes B12 and omega 3, the two nutrients plants cannot give you
the open edge in the old design: 55 kg/year of fish at feed conversion 1.5 to 2.0 eats 85 to 110 kg/year of feed that has to come from somewhere
token indoor cereal; worst per area indoor crop, kept minimal on purpose
3,100 kcal/day at the 4 to 6 t/ha this region actually yields; the data models it as a 2.4 m box, which is a marker not an area
700 kcal/day of protein AND the only real nitrogen input the homestead has
brings arable to 1,600 to 2,000 m2 (0.16 to 0.20 ha), which is FAO's global arable per capita of 0.19 ha
the four month winter light famine is eaten out of here; 2 to 5% storage loss in a sealed silo
roots and tubers lose 10 to 25% over a winter even when done well, which is why harvest must beat intake by about 15%
about 1.5 kWh/day; fresh food, frozen harvest surplus, ice cream in space
spices, teas, chamomile, aloe; flavour is a luxury loop worth closing
the only thing that beats the December light famine, at 10 to 50 kWh/day; the honest teaching meter shows the cost, and the cost is why the garden uses the sun

loops.name: Air
loops.demand: 0.77 kg/day (1.7 lb/day) of oxygen consumed and 0.92 kg/day (2.0 lb/day) of carbon dioxide produced, at the 2,600 kcal/day metabolic rate above. CORRECTED FROM 0.55 kg/day, which was 29 percent below even the old 2,200 kcal figure and 35 percent below NASA's nominal. Plus trace contaminant control, which the old outline had in neither tier.
loops.closure_note: NASA's standard crew metabolic values are 0.84 kg of oxygen and 1.00 kg of carbon dioxide per crew member per day at a metabolic rate of 136.7 W (11,200 Btu/day, 2,822 kcal/day) and a respiratory quotient of 0.87. Reproducing that from first principles as a check: 11.81 MJ/day divided by 20.3 kJ per litre of oxygen is 582 L, which at 1.429 g/L is 0.83 kg, so the method agrees with NASA and can be scaled. At this homestead's 2,600 kcal/day it gives 0.77 kg of oxygen and 0.92 kg of carbon dioxide. Can the garden do it? To release 0.77 kg of oxygen the canopy must fix 1.06 kg of carbon dioxide, which is 0.29 kg of carbon, which is about 0.72 kg of dry biomass a day. At about 1 g of dry biomass per mol of PAR that is 720 mol/day, which is 36 m2 (390 sq ft) of continuously closed canopy on the annual average light and 107 m2 (1,150 sq ft) in December, where the canopy is below the compensation point and is a net oxygen CONSUMER. BIOS-3 at Krasnoyarsk is the real anchor: 315 m3, 63 m2 (680 sq ft) of phytotron under xenon lamps, two to three crew, longest run 180 days, air regenerated to nearly 100 percent, water 85 to 95 percent, food only 50 to 80 percent. That is 20 to 30 m2 of intensely lit crop per person for air, which agrees with the 36 m2 calculation. THE CATCH NOBODY STATED: in a sealed volume, net oxygen production equals the rate at which fixed carbon is REMOVED from the loop. Composting 1.5 to 4 kg/day of residue inside the envelope is slow combustion and gives back almost exactly the oxygen that growing the residue released. BIOS-3 dried and stored its inedible biomass or oxidised it outside the loop for precisely this reason. So the old claim that 1,156 m2 of canopy makes far more oxygen than one person needs is wrong twice: the canopy is 44 m2, not 1,156, and even a correctly sized canopy only nets oxygen if you keep exporting carbon into the silo, into biochar, or out the airlock. On open Earth at this site none of this bites and the loop is free ventilation. In the sealed mothership case the loop closes only by budgeting about 5.8 kWh/day, which nothing in the old outline did: 5.0 kWh/day for electrolytic oxygen (1 kg of oxygen carries 0.125 kg of hydrogen and real electrolysers use 50 to 55 kWh per kg of hydrogen, so 6.5 kWh per kg of oxygen; the ISS oxygen generation assembly runs about 2 kW for six crew, which is 8 kWh/day per person for flight grade hardware), 0.6 kWh/day for a regenerable carbon dioxide sorbent bed, and 0.2 kWh/day for trace contaminant control. Compare the bioregenerative alternative: 720 mol of PAR a day from LEDs at 2.9 umol/J is 69 kWh/day, 17 times the bare minimum power budget. Electrolysis beats photosynthesis by about 12x on electricity, which is exactly why the ISS uses a machine and not a garden.
balance: Metabolic: 2,600 kcal/day = 10,879 kJ / 20.3 kJ per L O2 = 536 L O2/day x 1.429 g/L = 0.766 kg O2/day. CO2 at RQ 0.87 = 466 L x 1.977 g/L = 0.922 kg/day.
Method check against NASA: at 136.7 W (2,822 kcal/day) the same formula gives 0.83 kg O2/day against NASA's stated 0.84, and 1.00 kg CO2/day matching NASA exactly.
Old figure: 0.55 kg/day is 29% below the 0.65 kg/day that 2,200 kcal/day implies and 35% below NASA's 0.84 nominal.

Canopy needed for O2: 0.766 kg O2 needs 1.05 kg CO2 fixed = 0.287 kg C = 0.72 kg dry biomass; at 1 g/mol PAR that is 720 mol/day; at 20.2 mol/m2/day annual under glass = 36 m2; at 6.7 mol/m2/day December = 107 m2, and below compensation the canopy is net negative.
BIOS-3 anchor: 63 m2 of lit phytotron per 2 to 3 crew = 21 to 32 m2/person for near total air regeneration. Agrees with the 36 m2 calculation.

Composting penalty: aerobic composting of the 2.6 kg/day of crop residue oxidises roughly the same carbon the canopy fixed, so a sealed home that grows and composts inside the envelope nets close to zero oxygen.
Electrolytic O2: 0.766 kg O2 x 0.125 kg H2 per kg O2 = 0.096 kg H2 x 52 kWh/kg = 5.0 kWh/day. ISS OGA flight hardware: about 2 kW for 6 crew = 8 kWh/day per person.
CO2 removal: regenerable sorbent bed, ISS CDRA magnitude, 0.5 to 1.0 kWh/day per person. Point 0.6.

Trace contaminants: NASA TCCS is an activated charcoal bed plus a 400 C catalytic oxidiser plus a lithium hydroxide post sorbent at about 200 W = 0.2 kWh/day. HEPA is particulate only and removes none of it.
Sealed total: 5.0 + 0.6 + 0.2 = 5.8 kWh/day, which is 145% of the entire 4.0 kWh/day bare minimum power budget.
Bioregenerative alternative under LEDs: 720 mol/day / 2.9 umol/J = 248 MJ = 69 kWh/day. Electrolysis is about 12x cheaper.
assumptions: NASA crew metabolic baseline: 0.84 kg O2, 1.00 kg CO2, 0.62 kg food, 3.52 kg water per crew member per day at 136.7 W and respiratory quotient 0.87.
Energy equivalent of oxygen 20.3 kJ per litre at a mixed diet respiratory quotient.
BIOS-3, Institute of Biophysics, Krasnoyarsk, 1972 to 1984: 315 m3, 63 m2 phytotron, 1 to 3 crew, 180 day longest run, air near 100%, water 85 to 95%, food 50 to 80%.
Electrolyser 50 to 55 kWh per kg of hydrogen; horticultural LED efficacy 2.8 to 3.0 umol/J.
On open Earth at Silverdale this loop is free ventilation and everything above is the sealed habitat case only.

requirements.why: 25 W as catalogued, which is about an order of magnitude below what making 0.77 kg/day of oxygen actually costs; priority 1 on the bus for a reason
electrolysis at 6.5 kWh per kg of oxygen is 5.0 kWh/day for one person, more than the entire bare minimum power budget; this is the number the old outline never carried
0.92 kg/day of carbon dioxide has to go somewhere; a regenerable sorbent bed costs about 0.6 kWh/day
activated charcoal plus a catalytic oxidiser, about 0.2 kWh/day; a sealed box with a composter, a methane digester, solvents, and a kitchen needs gas phase control, and HEPA is particulate only

dust, pollen, and particulates only; it is comfort, not life support, and it was miscast as the trace contaminant answer
the boundary that turns air from free ventilation into a 5.8 kWh/day loop; on open Earth you do not need it and the loop is free

loops.name: Climate (heating and cooling)
loops.demand: Hold 20 C (68 F) year round against 2,610 heating degree days and 44 cooling degree days. For the 320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) house of the luxury tier the fabric plus ventilation heat loss coefficient is 182 W/K, so the annual heat demand is 11,400 kWh/year (36 kWh/m2/year), about 61 kWh/day gross on a January day and 48 kWh/day net of gains. For the 40 m2 (430 sq ft) bare minimum dwelling the same shell quality gives about 40 W/K and 2,500 kWh/year. Cooling is nearly a non-need at this site.
loops.closure_note: Insulation is the real machine and the shell numbers were never written down before, so here they are: 320 m2 of floor and 320 m2 of roof, 216 m2 of wall of which 32 m2 is glazing, at U values of 0.15 for walls, 0.10 for roof, 0.15 for floor, and 0.80 for triple glazing, gives a fabric loss of 133 W/K; 960 m3 at 0.35 air changes per hour through an 85 percent heat recovery ventilator plus 0.1 air changes of infiltration adds 49 W/K; total 182 W/K. Internal gains are real and worth counting: the occupant is a steady 100 W (2.4 kWh/day), all 4.0 kWh/day of bare minimum electricity lands indoors as heat, and 16 m2 of south glazing at 0.8 kWh/m2/day and a solar heat gain coefficient of 0.5 adds 6.4 kWh/day in December, about 12.8 kWh/day of gains in total. Bare minimum closes on the woodlot: 8,800 kWh of net heat over a 200 day season at 70 percent stove efficiency is 45.3 GJ of wood, which is 5.3 m3 of solid wood (2.2 cords) a year, which at a Pacific Northwest managed growth of 5 to 10 m3 per hectare per year is 0.53 to 1.06 ha (1.3 to 2.6 acres) of woodlot. That woodlot area is the number the old outline hid behind the phrase your own woodlot, and it is the largest piece of land in the whole design. CORRECTED, and this is the important one: the luxury heat pump was costed at about 5 kWh/day seasonal average, but 44 kWh/day of thermal at a coefficient of performance of 3.0 is 14.7 kWh/day electrical, and a December day at 48 kWh/day thermal and a real air source coefficient of 2.5 at 5 C is 19.2 kWh/day electrical, against a 14 panel array making 6.2 kWh/day that month. That is a threefold deficit on the heat pump alone. The 5 kWh/day figure is what a heat pump costs to heat about 100 m2, not 320 m2. The correction adopted here is the one a real off grid builder makes: deep winter stays on biomass, and the heat pump does shoulder seasons and summer cooling, where 12 kWh/day of thermal at a coefficient of 4.0 is 3 kWh/day electrical. Averaged across the year that IS about 5 kWh/day, so the old number was right for the duty the machine actually has and wrong for the duty the text implied. In the sealed mothership case the problem inverts entirely: there is no heating load at all and the question becomes heat rejection, where one occupant plus 16 kWh/day of equipment is 767 W needing about 4 m2 of radiator, while a glass roofed 4,895 m2 growing bay in full sun is roughly 4.9 MW needing on the order of 24,000 m2 of radiator, an order of magnitude larger problem than the house and one this outline had never mentioned.
balance: Ventilation: 960 m3 x 0.35 ACH = 336 m3/h = 112 W/K, x 0.15 after an 85% HRV = 16.8 W/K; plus 0.1 ACH infiltration = 32 W/K. Total 49 W/K.
Total 182 W/K. Annual heat = 182 x 2,610 C-days x 24 h = 11,400 kWh/year = 36 kWh/m2/year (Passive House is 15, a typical new US home is 100 to 150).
January: mean outdoor 5.5 C, delta T 14.5 K, 182 x 14.5 = 2,639 W = 63 kWh/day gross; minus 12.8 kWh/day of gains = 50 kWh/day net.
Heating season (200 days): 11,400 / 200 = 57 kWh/day gross, minus gains = 44 kWh/day net.

Wood: 44 x 200 = 8,800 kWh = 31.7 GJ delivered / 0.70 stove efficiency = 45.3 GJ of wood / 20.7 GJ per cord = 2.2 cords = 5.3 m3 solid/year; at 5 to 10 m3/ha/year growth that is 0.53 to 1.06 ha of woodlot.
Bare minimum 40 m2 dwelling: about 40 W/K, 2,500 kWh/year, about 1.2 m3 (0.5 cords) of wood on 0.12 to 0.24 ha. The 8x jump in floor area is the single biggest lever in this loop.
Luxury heat pump, corrected: 44 kWh/day thermal / COP 3.0 = 14.7 kWh/day electrical seasonal, 48 / 2.5 = 19.2 kWh/day in December, against 6.2 kWh/day from a 14 panel array. Deficit 13 kWh/day.

Heat pump on its real duty (shoulder season and cooling only): 12 kWh/day thermal / COP 4.0 = 3 kWh/day electrical, about 5 kWh/day averaged over the year. The stated number was right for this duty and wrong for full winter heating.
Cooling: 44 C cooling degree days. Shading, night ventilation, and thermal mass carry it; the spot air conditioner is a heat wave machine, not a season.

Sealed case: 100 W occupant + 667 W equipment = 767 W to reject; a 300 K radiator emits about 200 W/m2 net, so about 4 m2. A 4,895 m2 sunlit growing bay is about 4.9 MW, needing on the order of 24,000 m2 of radiator.
assumptions: House geometry from docs/design/homestead.md section 3: 16 x 20 m, 3 m ceilings, ten rooms.
2,610 C heating degree days base 18.3 C, converted from the 4,700 F day figure in location.ron.
Air source heat pump COP 2.5 at 5 C outdoor, 3.0 seasonal heating average, 4.0 in shoulder conditions.
Seasoned Douglas fir at about 20.7 GJ per cord, wood stove efficiency 0.70, managed Pacific Northwest woodlot growth 5 to 10 m3 per hectare per year.
Radiator emission taken at 200 W/m2 net for a 300 K surface with emissivity 0.9 and a 50% view factor.

requirements.why: walls U 0.15, roof U 0.10, floor U 0.15, triple glazing U 0.80, heat recovery at 85%; every other climate number scales off this one
5.3 m3 (2.2 cords) of wood a year off 0.53 to 1.06 ha (1.3 to 2.6 acres) of woodlot; the ash is also the only potassium the nutrient loop gets back
the largest single piece of land in the design, and it was hidden behind the words your own woodlot
6.4 kWh/day of December gain at a solar heat gain coefficient of 0.5, half the total internal gains, for no power at all
turns 112 W/K of ventilation loss into 17 W/K; without it the ventilation term alone is most of the heating bill in a tight house
about 3 kWh/day on its real duty and about 5 kWh/day averaged annually; running it through December instead would take 19.2 kWh/day and break the array
44 cooling degree days means this is a heat wave and server corner machine, not a season
warm feet, silent, and low grade heat is exactly what the heat pump makes most efficiently
schedules the whole loop around occupancy and the solar forecast, which matters most in the month the array is tightest

loops.name: Nutrients and waste
loops.demand: About 4.3 kg/day (9.5 lb/day) of organic material back to the soil: 1.5 kg of human excreta, 0.2 kg of kitchen scraps, and 2.6 kg of wet crop residue. CORRECTED FROM 1.5 kg/day, which counted excreta only while the text said food scraps, crop residue, and humanure. In nutrient terms the crops take up about 7.9 kg of nitrogen, 1.3 kg of phosphorus, and 10.5 kg of potassium a year, and that is the balance that has to be met.
loops.closure_note: THIS LOOP DOES NOT CLOSE, and saying so is the point. The old claim was that compost plus urine diversion return 587 percent of the nitrogen, 533 percent of the phosphorus, and 197 percent of the potassium the crops need. Those figures appear nowhere in this repository with a derivation and cannot be reproduced from any mass balance. Working it honestly: one person's complete diet is about 650 g/day of edible dry matter, which at a garden wide harvest index of 0.45 means 527 kg/year of total plant dry matter, which at whole plant contents of 1.5 percent nitrogen, 0.25 percent phosphorus, and 2.0 percent potassium is an uptake of 7.9 kg N, 1.3 kg P, and 10.5 kg K a year. Coming back: human excreta supply about 4.0 kg N, 0.6 kg P, and 1.2 kg K per person year (published ranges 2.5 to 4.3, 0.4 to 1.0, and 0.9 to 1.4, from the Swedish source separation literature); composted crop residue recycles about 4.4 kg N, 0.7 kg P, and 5.8 kg K, though that is internal recycling and not a new input; and wood ash from 2.2 cords adds about 0.9 kg K. Composting then loses 20 to 40 percent of the nitrogen as ammonia and 5 to 15 percent of the phosphorus and potassium to leaching. Net returned: 5.9 kg N (75 percent of uptake), 1.17 kg P (90 percent), and 6.9 kg K (66 percent). So the honest figures are roughly 75, 90, and 66 percent, against claims of 587, 533, and 197 percent, which are off by about 8x, 6x, and 3x. Nitrogen can be closed, because legumes fix it, but the 2.0 kg/year gap needs about 200 m2 of legume land dedicated purely to nitrogen at 100 kg per hectare per year, on top of the legume grown for food, and the legume_field as sized in the data (5.76 m2) fixes about 3 percent of that. Potassium is numerically the tightest at a 3.6 kg/year gap, and wood ash is the only on site source and covers 0.9 kg of it. Phosphorus is the one that can never be closed in principle, because there is no biological phosphorus fixation: nothing on the homestead makes phosphorus, so the 0.13 kg/year leaching loss is permanent. And export is the term that decides everything. The design banks a 3,100 kcal/day grain surplus for trade; if about 1,900 kcal/day of that is genuinely traded away, that is 209 kg of wheat a year leaving the farm carrying 4.4 kg of nitrogen, 0.73 kg of phosphorus, and 0.84 kg of potassium, which exceeds everything the resident's own body returns. Trading calories is trading soil. Over 25 years at that rate the homestead ships out about 18 kg of phosphorus it has to buy back as mined rock phosphate. That does not close a cannot close loop; it puts a number on why raw chemistry is on that list.
balance: Uptake: 650 g/day edible dry matter = 237 kg/year; at harvest index 0.45 total plant dry matter = 527 kg/year. At N 1.5%, P 0.25%, K 2.0%: N 7.9, P 1.3, K 10.5 kg/year.
Excreta return: N 4.0, P 0.6, K 1.2 kg/person-year (ranges 2.5 to 4.3, 0.4 to 1.0, 0.9 to 1.4).
Residue return (290 kg/year dry, internal recycling only): N 4.4, P 0.7, K 5.8 kg/year.
Wood ash from 2.2 cords: about 22 kg ash at 6% K2O = 0.9 kg K, plus calcium and a trace of phosphorus.
Composting losses: N minus 30% (range 20 to 40, as ammonia), P and K minus 10% (range 5 to 15, leaching).
Net to beds: N 5.9, P 1.17, K 6.9 kg/year. Against uptake: N 75%, P 90%, K 66%. Claimed: 587%, 533%, 197%.
Nitrogen gap 2.0 kg/year needs about 200 m2 of dedicated legume at 100 kg N per hectare per year. The legume_field in the data is 5.76 m2 and fixes about 0.06 kg N/year, about 3% of the gap.
Potassium gap 3.6 kg/year. Wood ash covers 0.9 kg. Residual 2.7 kg/year is traded in as mineral potash.
Phosphorus gap 0.13 kg/year with zero export, and there is no biological phosphorus fixation at all, so the deficit is permanent rather than recoverable.

Export term: 1,900 kcal/day of traded wheat = 574 g/day = 209 kg/year at N 2.1%, P 0.35%, K 0.40% = N 4.4, P 0.73, K 0.84 kg/year leaving the farm, which is more nitrogen and phosphorus than the resident's body returns.

Compost mass check: 4.3 kg/day of wet feedstock losing 60 to 70% to water and carbon dioxide gives 1.3 to 1.7 kg/day of finished compost, so the catalogued +1.2 kg/day figure is correct as COMPOST and wrong by about 70x as NUTRIENT. Actual nutrient in 1.2 kg of compost at 1.5% N, 0.5% P, 1.0% K is 18 g N, 6 g P, 12 g K per day.
assumptions: Excreta nutrient figures from the source separation literature (Vinneras and Jonsson 2002; Jonsson et al. 2004, EcoSanRes Guidelines on the Use of Urine and Faeces in Crop Production).
Whole plant nutrient contents N 1.5%, P 0.25%, K 2.0% of dry matter, a garden wide average across grain, legume, root, and leaf crops.
Biological nitrogen fixation 50 to 150 kg per hectare per year for a well managed legume crop; point estimate 100.
Wood ash 0.5 to 1.5% of wood mass at 3 to 9% K2O; point estimate 1.0% and 6%.
The balance is stated with and without the traded grain surplus, because export is what flips the sign.

requirements.why: 1.2 kg/day of finished COMPOST, which carries about 18 g N, 6 g P, 12 g K, plus 59 L/day (16 gal/day) of greywater; the second bin bridges the 60 to 90 day maturation lag
urine carries most of the nitrogen and potassium a body returns, and diverting it avoids the 20 to 40% ammonia loss that composting causes
blackwater handling; note that anything that leaves here leaves the nutrient loop as well
the only true nitrogen input the homestead has; the 2.0 kg/year gap needs this much land at 100 kg N per hectare per year
0.9 kg of the 3.6 kg/year potassium gap, and the only on site potassium source there is

requirements.qty: 0.13 to 0.86 kg P and 2.7 kg K per year
requirements.why: THE LOOP THAT DOES NOT CLOSE: no biological process makes phosphorus, so every gram lost or traded away is bought back from a mine. See the raw chemistry entry below
about 0.25 m3/day of biogas, roughly 0.37 kWh/day of electricity, plus digestate; useful, but about a third of the winter generator fuel rather than all of it
the only way to bank carbon out of a sealed air loop while keeping the minerals; composting inside a sealed envelope gives the oxygen straight back

loops.name: Shelter and workshop
loops.demand: Bare minimum 40 m2 (430 sq ft) of floor and 100 m3 (3,500 cu ft) of volume for one person; life of luxury the ten room house this design actually draws, 320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) on a 16 x 20 m (52 x 66 ft) block with 3 m (10 ft) ceilings, 960 m3 (33,900 cu ft). In a sealed habitat never go below about 25 m3 (880 cu ft) of net habitable volume per person. Land, all in, one person at this site: greenhouse 350 m2, arable including rotation 1,600 to 2,000 m2, woodlot 5,300 to 10,600 m2, house and yard 500 m2, which is about 0.8 to 1.3 ha (2 to 3 acres).
loops.closure_note: The house is the container that makes every other loop's numbers work, and it had no numbers of its own until now. The bare minimum floor area is grounded in the UK Nationally Described Space Standard, which sets 39 m2 for a one bedroom one person dwelling, and for the sealed case in NASA's net habitable volume guidance, which puts the long duration lower limit near 25 m3 per person while the ISS actually provides about 100 m3 per crew member. BIOS-3 ran 315 m3 for one to three crew. The 8x jump between the two tiers, 40 m2 against 320 m2, is the single largest lever in the climate loop: it is the difference between 1.2 m3 (0.5 cords) and 5.3 m3 (2.2 cords) of firewood a year, and between 0.12 ha and 1.06 ha of woodlot. Nothing else in this outline moves a number that hard. The land total is worth sitting with: the arable line of 0.16 to 0.20 ha lands exactly on FAO's global arable per capita of 0.19 ha, which is a reassuring independent check, and the woodlot is what makes the total large, so it is also the term that disappears the moment you stop heating with wood. The workshop is what keeps every other machine alive, and at the luxury tier it also makes things: printed spare parts, custom brackets, repaired boards. What it cannot make is the panel's cells, the battery's cells, the pump's windings, or any circuit board, which is the equipment replacement entry in the panel below and is unchanged by this audit.
balance: Bare minimum dwelling: 40 m2 x 2.5 m = 100 m3. UK Nationally Described Space Standard sets 39 m2 for a one bed one person dwelling.
Sealed floor: NASA net habitable volume guidance puts the long duration lower limit near 25 m3 per person; ISS provides about 100 m3 per crew; BIOS-3 was 315 m3 for 1 to 3 crew.
Luxury dwelling: 16 x 20 m = 320 m2 x 3 m = 960 m3 across ten rooms (docs/design/homestead.md section 3).
Climate consequence: 40 m2 gives about 40 W/K and 2,500 kWh/year of heat; 320 m2 gives 182 W/K and 11,400 kWh/year. Wood goes from 0.5 cords to 2.2 cords a year.
Land: greenhouse 350 m2 + arable 1,600 to 2,000 m2 + woodlot 5,300 to 10,600 m2 + house and yard 500 m2 = 7,750 to 13,450 m2, about 0.8 to 1.3 ha (2 to 3 acres).
Cross-check: the arable line of 0.16 to 0.20 ha matches FAO's global arable per capita of 0.19 ha.
assumptions: Minimum dwelling area from the UK Nationally Described Space Standard (39 m2, one bedroom, one person).
Sealed habitable volume from NASA long duration net habitable volume guidance, floor about 25 m3 per person.
House geometry from docs/design/homestead.md section 3, which is the shell the machine files already place instances inside.
Land totals assume wood heating; drop the woodlot and the total falls to about 0.25 to 0.29 ha.

requirements.why: the 8x spread between the tiers is the biggest single lever on the heating bill in the whole design
sink, shower, toilet; between them they are 54 of the 85 L/day the water loop balances
the four month winter light famine is survived here, not in the garden
repairs keep every other loop's machines alive, and repair is the only part of equipment renewal a homestead actually owns
greenhouse 350 m2, arable 1,600 to 2,000 m2, woodlot 5,300 to 10,600 m2, house and yard 500 m2; the woodlot is most of it
about 0.2 kWh/day averaged; prints the brackets, knobs, and jigs that would otherwise be a supply run
about 0.5 kWh/day averaged across saws, drills, welder; hours become minutes
about 1.5 kWh/day; work, games, movies, and the home's own automation brain

cannot_close.note: Five loops stay open no matter how good the homestead is: electronics and semiconductors, metal from raw ore, medicine synthesis, equipment replacement, and raw chemistry inputs. This audit did not close any of them and made one of them sharper: the nutrients loop above puts a real number on the phosphorus gap, which is the raw chemistry entry. The gap is not a failure; it is why neighbors, trade, and civilization exist.

footer: Six of these seven loops close, and the seventh, nutrients, does not, which is the most useful thing on this page. A single person can close energy, water, air, climate, and food at a named place with stated assumptions, and the moment they trade a calorie surplus they start exporting soil. Every number above is a balance you can check, and several of them were wrong until someone did.
